parrafos: Lithium, cobalt, nickel, copper and a handful of obscure elements known collectively as rare earths have quietly become the new oil of geopolitics. Governments that for decades were content to leave mining to markets are now drafting industrial strategies, building stockpiles and courting producers on the other side of the world. Whether this frantic race delivers genuine security or merely higher costs is far from settled, yet its outcome will shape the energy transition for a generation.

The logic behind the rush is simple enough. An electric car needs several times more minerals than a conventional one, and an onshore wind farm far more than a gas-fired power station of similar capacity. Batteries, solar panels, transmission lines and data centres all draw on the same narrow list of raw materials. According to most international projections, demand for lithium could multiply several-fold by the end of the next decade, while demand for copper, the workhorse of electrification, is expected to outpace anything existing mines can supply.

The difficulty lies less in geology than in geography and, above all, in processing. Deposits of most critical minerals are reasonably widespread, but extraction is concentrated in a few countries: a large share of the world’s cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of Congo, and much of its lithium from Australia and the so-called lithium triangle of Chile, Argentina and Bolivia. Refining is more concentrated still. China processes well over half of the world’s lithium and cobalt and the overwhelming majority of its rare earths, a dominance built patiently over three decades while others looked away.

That dominance was long regarded as a mere commercial fact. It has since become a strategic concern. Beijing has shown that it is willing to restrict exports of certain metals, such as gallium and germanium, as well as of the technologies used to process rare earths, in response to Western controls on advanced semiconductors. For manufacturers in Europe and America, the lesson was sobering: a single licensing decision taken in another capital can halt a production line thousands of kilometres away.

Western governments have responded with a flurry of initiatives. The European Union adopted a Critical Raw Materials Act that sets non-binding targets: by 2030 it hopes to extract around a tenth of its annual consumption at home, process about two-fifths and recycle a quarter, while ensuring that no single third country supplies more than about two-thirds of any strategic material. The United States has tied generous tax credits for electric vehicles to the origin of battery components, and has even taken stakes in mining and refining companies. Japan, which learned its lesson after a rare-earths dispute with China more than a decade ago, has long maintained public stockpiles and financed projects abroad.

Yet ambition collides with stubborn realities. Opening a new mine in Europe typically takes well over a decade once exploration, environmental assessment, permitting and legal challenges are counted. Local opposition is often fierce: projects in Portugal, Spain and Serbia have met protests from residents worried about water, landscapes and tourism. The paradox is plain. Many of the same citizens who support the green transition in principle are reluctant to host the quarries and refineries it requires, preferring that the dirty work be done elsewhere.

Money is another obstacle. Mineral prices are notoriously volatile, and the recent past offers a cautionary tale. After a spectacular boom, lithium prices collapsed by more than three-quarters within a couple of years, as new supply flooded in and sales of electric cars grew more slowly than expected. Western projects with higher costs were mothballed, while Chinese producers, often backed by state banks, could weather the storm. Investors have drawn the obvious conclusion: without some form of price floor or guaranteed buyer, building capacity outside China is a risky bet.

Hence the growing interest in partnerships with producer countries. Europe and America have signed strategic agreements with nations from Chile to Indonesia and from Namibia to Kazakhstan, promising investment and technical assistance in exchange for access. The producers, however, have learned from history. Indonesia banned exports of raw nickel ore to force smelting to take place on its own soil, and several Latin American governments are seeking a larger share of the value created, through state-owned companies or higher royalties. Resource nationalism, in short, is back, and buyers can no longer dictate terms.

Recycling offers a partial escape. Spent batteries, scrapped electronics and industrial waste contain significant quantities of valuable metals, and recovering them reduces both imports and environmental damage. But the stock of material available for recycling is still small, because most electric cars on the road are young and will not be scrapped for years. Recycling will matter enormously in the long run; in the coming decade it can only complement new extraction, not replace it.

Technology may also ease the pressure. Battery makers have already shifted part of their production towards chemistries that use less cobalt or none at all, and sodium-based batteries could reduce reliance on lithium for some uses. History suggests that scarcity tends to stimulate substitution: when a material becomes expensive or risky, engineers find ways to economise on it. Some economists therefore warn against overestimating the danger, and against costly subsidies that could lock in today’s technologies just as better ones are emerging.

The real risk may be of a different nature. If each bloc pursues self-sufficiency through subsidies, export bans and local-content rules, the result could be a fragmented market in which minerals are dearer for everyone and the energy transition proceeds more slowly. Diversification, which means building several reliable sources rather than relying on one, is a sensible insurance policy. Autarky, by contrast, is a costly illusion, particularly for a region as poor in mineral resources as Europe.

The scramble for critical minerals is therefore not simply a race for rocks. It is a test of whether governments can combine industrial policy with open trade, environmental standards with faster permitting, and strategic caution with economic common sense. Those who strike this balance will secure the materials of the future; those who do not may discover that they have swapped their dependence on fossil fuels for a new and no less uncomfortable one.
resumen_es: Analysis of the competition between powers for lithium, cobalt and rare earths: dependence on China, the responses of the EU and the US, and the limits of self-sufficiency.

ideas_clave.idea: Because the energy transition multiplies the need for metals such as lithium and copper, states that once left mining to the market now treat these materials as a strategic priority.
The main vulnerability is that refining is dominated by China, which has already used export restrictions as a political weapon.
The EU has set targets for domestic extraction, processing, recycling and supplier diversification, while the US and Japan rely on subsidies, public stakes and stockpiles.
New mines in Europe face long approval procedures and local resistance, even from people who back the green transition.
Price volatility, illustrated by the collapse of lithium, makes Western projects unprofitable without public guarantees.
Agreements with producer countries are complicated by a return of resource nationalism, as these countries demand more local processing and revenue.
Recycling and technological substitution can relieve the pressure, but recycling will only become significant in the long term.
The greatest danger is a fragmented market driven by protectionism; diversification is sensible, whereas self-sufficiency is unattainable for Europe.
The challenge is to reconcile industrial policy and open trade so as not to replace one energy dependence with another.

resumen_modelo: The text examines the growing competition among major economies for critical minerals such as lithium, cobalt, copper and rare earths. Since electric vehicles, renewable energy and power grids require far larger quantities of these materials, demand is set to soar, and governments have abandoned their former reliance on markets. The core problem is not the scarcity of deposits but the concentration of extraction in a few countries and, above all, China’s overwhelming control of refining, which Beijing has shown it is prepared to use as leverage through export restrictions. In response, the European Union has adopted non-binding targets for domestic mining, processing, recycling and supplier diversification, while Washington offers tax incentives and acquires stakes in companies, and Tokyo maintains stockpiles. These efforts nevertheless face serious obstacles: lengthy permitting, local opposition to mines, and highly volatile prices, as the recent collapse of lithium demonstrated, which deter private investment. Partnerships with producer countries are also harder to strike, since many now insist on processing their resources at home. Recycling and new battery chemistries may ease the pressure, although the former will only make a real contribution in the long run. The author concludes that the main risk lies in a fragmented, protectionist market that would raise costs for everyone. Diversifying suppliers is therefore prudent, whereas pursuing self-sufficiency would be an expensive illusion, particularly for Europe.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: According to the author, it is already clear that the race for minerals will provide greater security.
preguntas.cita: Whether this frantic race delivers genuine security or merely higher costs is far from settled
preguntas.explicacion: The author says the outcome is “far from settled”: it may bring security or merely higher costs. So the statement is false.

preguntas.pregunta: According to the text, where does the main difficulty in the supply of critical minerals lie?
opciones: In the scarcity of deposits around the world
In the concentration of extraction and, above all, of processing
In the lack of demand from manufacturers
In the high cost of transporting ores by sea
respuestas: In the concentration of extraction and, above all, of processing
preguntas.cita: The difficulty lies less in geology than in geography and, above all, in processing.
preguntas.explicacion: The text states that deposits are “reasonably widespread”, so scarcity is not the problem. Transport and lack of demand are not mentioned; the problem is the geographical concentration of mining and refining.

preguntas.enunciado: Find an expression in paragraph 3 that means “while the others were not paying attention”.
preguntas.pregunta: Find an expression meaning ‘while others paid no attention’.
preguntas.cita: a dominance built patiently over three decades while others looked away
preguntas.explicacion: “Look away” means to turn your eyes away; here it indicates that other countries did not deal with the issue while China was building its dominance.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: China has restricted exports of some metals as a reaction to Western controls on advanced chips.
preguntas.cita: in response to Western controls on advanced semiconductors
preguntas.explicacion: The paragraph says that Beijing has restricted exports of gallium, germanium and rare-earth technologies in response to Western controls on advanced semiconductors.

preguntas.pregunta: What characterises the targets of the EU Critical Raw Materials Act as described in the text?
opciones: They are legally binding for all member states
They are non-binding goals for extraction, processing, recycling and diversification
They ban imports of strategic materials from China
They only concern the recycling of batteries
respuestas: They are non-binding goals for extraction, processing, recycling and diversification
preguntas.explicacion: The text says explicitly that the targets are “non-binding” and cover extraction, processing, recycling and a cap on dependence on a single country. It does not ban imports or focus only on recycling.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Japan started building public stockpiles only recently, after Europe adopted its law.
preguntas.cita: has long maintained public stockpiles and financed projects abroad
preguntas.explicacion: Japan “has long maintained” public stockpiles, since a dispute with China more than a decade ago; it is neither recent nor a reaction to the European law.

preguntas.enunciado: Find a word in paragraph 6 that means “open-air sites where stone or minerals are dug out” (es: canteras).
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning ‘open pits from which stone or minerals are extracted’.
preguntas.cita: are reluctant to host the quarries and refineries it requires
preguntas.explicacion: A “quarry” is an open-pit site for extracting stone (es: cantera); the text uses it together with “refineries” to refer to the facilities the transition requires.

preguntas.pregunta: Why were some Western lithium projects put on hold?
opciones: Because environmental groups won lawsuits against them
Because lithium prices fell sharply and their costs were higher
Because China bought the companies that owned them
Because the EU withdrew its subsidies
respuestas: Because lithium prices fell sharply and their costs were higher
preguntas.cita: Western projects with higher costs were mothballed
preguntas.explicacion: After the collapse in the lithium price, the more expensive Western projects were “mothballed”. The text does not mention lawsuits, Chinese purchases or the withdrawal of European subsidies.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Indonesia prohibited the export of unprocessed nickel ore.
preguntas.cita: Indonesia banned exports of raw nickel ore to force smelting to take place on its own soil
preguntas.explicacion: The text states it word for word: Indonesia banned exports of unprocessed nickel ore so that smelting would take place on its territory.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Recycling already covers most of Europe’s demand for battery metals.
preguntas.cita: the stock of material available for recycling is still small
preguntas.explicacion: The text says that the material available for recycling is still scarce and that over the next decade recycling can only complement extraction.

preguntas.enunciado: Find a verb in paragraph 10 that means “to save, to use less of something”.
preguntas.pregunta: Find a verb meaning ‘to use less of something’.
preguntas.cita: engineers find ways to economise on it
preguntas.explicacion: “Economise on something” means to save on or reduce the use of something; British spelling with -ise.

preguntas.pregunta: What does the author consider the real risk?
opciones: A complete halt of Chinese exports
A fragmented market caused by each bloc seeking self-sufficiency
The exhaustion of global lithium deposits
respuestas: A fragmented market caused by each bloc seeking self-sufficiency
preguntas.cita: the result could be a fragmented market in which minerals are dearer for everyone
preguntas.explicacion: The author places the real risk in the fragmentation of the market caused by the pursuit of self-sufficiency. He does not mention the depletion of deposits or a total halt to Chinese exports.

preguntas.enunciado: Answer in your own words (1–3 sentences).
preguntas.pregunta: What paradox does the author identify regarding public attitudes to mining in Europe?
respuestas: Many Europeans support the green transition in principle but oppose mines and refineries near their homes, even though the transition depends on them; they would rather the extraction took place in other countries.
preguntas.cita: Many of the same citizens who support the green transition in principle are reluctant to host the quarries and refineries it requires
preguntas.explicacion: The paradox is that citizens support the green transition but reject the facilities that make it possible, preferring the pollution to stay elsewhere.

preguntas.enunciado: Answer in your own words (1–3 sentences).
preguntas.pregunta: Why does the author say that the scramble is ‘not simply a race for rocks’?
respuestas: Because it is really a test of governments’ ability to balance competing goals: industrial policy and free trade, environmental protection and faster approvals, security and economic efficiency. Failing could create a new dependence similar to the one on fossil fuels.
preguntas.cita: It is a test of whether governments can combine industrial policy with open trade
preguntas.explicacion: The conclusion presents the race as a test of political and economic balance, not as a mere competition for physical resources.
